title: GeneMamba: Efficient and Effective Foundation Model on Single Cell Data.
abstract: Transformer-based models have achieved strong performance in single-cell transcriptomics, yet scaling them to genome-wide gene sequences remains challenging due to the quadratic cost of self-attention. Recent state space models (SSMs) offer linear-time sequence modeling, but unidirectional designs may introduce ordering biases and overlook biological structure, potentially limiting robustness across datasets. To address these challenges, we propose GeneMamba, a bidirectional state space model tailored for single-cell RNA sequencing. GeneMamba integrates three key components: (1) Efficiency: BiMamba blocks enable bidirectional processing with O(L) complexity, providing substantial speedup over transformer baselines while maintaining linear scaling; (2) Biological integration: a pathway-aware contrastive objective incorporates curated pathway information to guide representation learning; (3) Scalability: large-scale pretraining on approximately 30 million curated cells (from ~50 million raw CELLXGENE profiles) supports transfer across multiple downstream tasks without task-specific architectures. Across benchmarks including multi-batch integration, cell type annotation, and gene rank reconstruction, GeneMamba demonstrates competitive performance relative to strong baselines such as scGPT and Geneformer, with improvements observed in several settings. Ablation studies further suggest that bidirectional modeling and pathway-aware pretraining contribute to these gains. Overall, GeneMamba provides an efficient and biologically informed framework for foundation modeling in single-cell transcriptomics.

title: An autoencoder outperforms two transformers on prediction of gene expression from chromatin accessibility
abstract: Models that predict RNA abundance from chromatin accessibility are rarely compared under the same features, targets and metrics. We built one benchmark on 126,604 paired single-nucleus profiles from 19 human studies with a shared vocabulary of 50,000 peaks and 3,185 genes, ten 5x2 cross-validation folds and one scoring target, and compared seven implemented pipelines and two reference predictors across 70 trained runs; each pipeline keeps its own input normalisation and native training target. The scButterfly-B pipeline, built on dual variational autoencoders, outperformed every transformer pipeline, including an autoregressive Perceiver model (Omic Translator) and a support-free reformulation of Cisformer, on per-gene and within-cell Spearman correlation in all sixty paired fold comparisons, with 3.8 times shorter training. Transformer pipelines come within 0.02-0.04 on within-cell profile shape but lag by 0.10-0.24 on per-gene correlation. On two withheld cell types per-gene correlation is low; controls show the podocyte values are typical of within-type correlation for seen cell types of the same size, whereas Paneth values match a cell-agnostic shuffle for every Omic Translator arm. Within the transformer family, prespecified ablations show the Perceiver encoder was worth +0.0439 in within-donor per-gene correlation over full self-attention, a chromosome-aware genomic attention prior reduced it by 0.0096 (exact donor-level sign-flip test, Holm-adjusted p = 1.2e-4), and decoder output order had no detectable effect. A training-mean profile reaches 0.314 within-cell correlation with no input and a constant at the true expressed-gene positions reaches 0.996 per-gene correlation, so oracle-support protocols are reported only as diagnostics. Code, results and an audited release are provided.

title: Small variant calling in the era of long-read sequencing.
abstract: Long-read sequencing enables accurate analysis of complex and repetitive genomic regions but has distinct error profiles compared to short-read sequencing. Consequently, the tools for calling small variants - the predominant source of human genetic diversity - have shifted towards deep learning-based methods. This transition has reshaped variant calling across biological contexts, including germline, de novo, somatic and mosaic variants, and sequencing modalities for capturing both DNA and RNA at different resolutions. These deep learning frameworks are being developed in combination with alignment-based, assembly-based and pangenome-based strategies for small variant detection. In this Review, we chart the trajectory towards complete telomere-to-telomere profiling of small variants and consider the computational innovations needed to benchmark newly accessible repetitive regions and complex variants.

title: Long Non-Coding RNAs: Key Regulators of Economic Traits in Livestock From Mechanisms to Breeding Applications.
abstract: Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) have emerged as critical regulators of economically important traits in livestock, including growth, reproduction, disease resistance and product quality. Unlike protein-coding genes, lncRNAs orchestrate gene expression at epigenetic, transcriptional and post-transcriptional levels, acting as molecular switches, scaffolds, decoys, and competing endogenous RNAs (ceRNAs). This review synthesises current knowledge on key lncRNA mechanisms such as ceRNA networks, liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) and RNA-targeting clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR-Cas13) screening alongside trait-specific case studies in muscle hypertrophy (Callipyge locus), embryonic development (lnc_2217 in goats) and fecundity (ceRNA networks in sheep and chickens). We highlight the integration of lncRNAs with Genome Wide Association Studies (GWAS) data, where over 90% of trait-associated variants reside in non-coding regions, and propose a practical roadmap for functional validation and incorporation of lncRNAs into genomic selection and breeding programs. Harnessing lncRNA biology supported by recent functional annotation of animal genomes (FAANG) epigenomic maps and CRISPR-Cas13 applications in livestock, researchers will accelerate genetic gain in growth rate, marbling score, litter size and disease resilience, marking a paradigm shift toward precision livestock breeding.

title: One Health surveillance of bat virome in mainland Southeast Asia and adjacent regions.
abstract: Bats are critical viral reservoirs that harbor viromes with high cross-species transmission risks, yet their virome diversity in the mainland Southeast Asia and adjacent regions remains underexplored. Here, we characterized the bat viromes from 659 samples (197 individuals, 16 species) from Yunnan province and Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region, China, as well as from Cambodia, using next-generation sequencing (NGS). RNA sequencing, viral classification, phylogenetic analyses, and deep learning-based host adaptability analysis were performed to reveal the viral composition and cross-species transmission risks. We identified 137 viral strains, including 40 novel species spanning 18 families. Viral richness was highest in Vespertilionidae bats (12 viral families found) along China's southwestern border, where Middle Eastern respiratory syndrome (MERS)-like coronavirus (CoV) was found. Cambodian bat viruses were evolutionarily more distant from those of known viruses. A porcine epidemic diarrhea virus (PEDV)-related CoV was found in Cambodia, showing 90.36% genome homology with PEDV CV777 and exhibiting recombinant features between Suidae-adapted ORF1ab and Chiroptera-adapted Spike genes, suggesting that bats are the evolutionary source of PEDV. These findings illuminate the undercharacterized bat viral diversity in biogeographic transition zones and highlight the mainland Southeast Asia and adjacent regions as a hotspot for CoV recombination. We advocate for enhanced One Health-aligned surveillance targeting viral recombination hotspots and human-bat interfaces in this ecologically critical region.

title: LncRNA-protein interactions: molecular switches for the precise regulation of innate immunity.
abstract: Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) have emerged as important regulators of innate immunity, acting across multiple molecular layers to shape antiviral and inflammatory responses. Among their diverse functions, protein-centered regulation provides a particularly versatile means of controlling immune signaling by altering the functional state, interactions, localization, or turnover of proteins without necessarily changing their transcription. In this review, we synthesize current evidence for lncRNA-mediated protein regulation in innate immunity and propose a protein-centered framework that connects molecular regulatory mechanisms with their functional and immunological consequences. At the mechanistic level, lncRNA-protein interactions can modulate post-translational modifications, alter protein conformations, and facilitate or disrupt protein-protein interactions. These regulatory modes, in turn, affect four major properties of immune proteins: protein stability, subcellular localization, molecular activity, and protein-protein interaction-dependent signal transmission, ultimately reshaping innate immune responses. Across these mechanisms, several recurrent principles emerge, including preferential regulation of functionally important signaling nodes, integration of multiple regulatory mechanisms, and strong dependence on cellular and immunological context. Emerging evidence further suggests that some lncRNAs may act on defined protein states or regulatory interfaces without altering total protein abundance, although the generality of such functional selectivity remains to be established. Together, these findings support a hierarchical model in which lncRNAs translate specific molecular interactions into changes in protein function and, ultimately, innate immune states. This framework provides a basis for understanding how lncRNA-protein interactions contribute to the fine-tuning of innate immunity and for evaluating their potential as targets for selective immune modulation.

title: Migrasome-driven mitocytosis relieves mitochondrial damage induced by chikungunya virus TF and 6K.
abstract: Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) infection induces the formation of migrasomes, yet their specific role in CHIKV pathogenesis remains unclear. This study explores the mechanisms underlying mitochondrial damage induced by CHIKV 181 clone 25 (CHIKV 181/25) and the role of migrasomes in mitigating this damage. Using cultured cell lines, we assessed the impact of CHIKV infection on mitochondrial integrity and function, with particular emphasis on the viroporin proteins transframe (TF) and 6K. We utilized fluorescence microscopy and transmission electron microscopy to visualize the interplay between migrasome formation and damaged mitochondria. Additionally, calcium imaging assays were conducted to evaluate intracellular calcium levels, and RNA sequencing was performed to examine gene expression. Our results demonstrated that CHIKV infection leads to mitochondrial damage, mediated by the action of TF and 6K. Notably, migrasomes induced by nonstructural protein 1 (nsP1) effectively clearing impaired mitochondria through mitocytosis. Furthermore, we identified the arginine residue R37 within the viroporin proteins of CHIKV as crucial for inducing mitochondrial damage through elevated intracellular calcium levels. Importantly, R37 within TF from other alphaviruses is also critical for mitochondrial damage. In conclusion, our findings elucidate the complex interplay between CHIKV and mitochondrial dysfunction, positioning migrasomes as potential mediators in alleviating CHIKV-induced mitochondrial damage.

title: Shape-Dependent Interactions of Gold Nanoparticles with Microalgae: Distinct Cellular and Molecular Responses.
abstract: The ecotoxicological effects of engineered nanoparticles in aquatic environments are influenced not only by composition and size but also by particle morphology, yet shape-dependent interactions with primary producers remain poorly understood. In this study, we evaluated the cellular and molecular responses of freshwater algae (Chlamydomonas reinhardtii) following exposure to 100 nm silica-coated gold nanospheres (AuNPs) and nanostars (AuNSs) across multiple concentrations. Exposure to 10 mg/L AuNSs for 72 h results in significantly stronger inhibition of algal growth and photosynthetic activity compared to the same concentration of AuNPs. Morphometric profiling reveals that AuNSs induce pronounced structural injury, including cell enlargement, debris production, and disruption of subcellular organization, more than AuNPs. Confocal imaging suggested that this heightened toxicity may stem from two distinct internalization patterns: AuNPs primarily adhered to chloroplast surfaces, whereas AuNSs caused more extensive membrane disruption and were observed deeper within intracellular compartments. RNA sequencing identified 9 upregulated and 38 downregulated differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in the 10 mg/L AuNP-treated cells, impairing photosynthesis and energy storage via the photosystem II subunit S1 (PSBS1)/early light-inducible protein (ELI3) pathway. In contrast, the AuNS group exhibits 246 upregulated and 145 downregulated DEGs, affecting membrane integrity and nitrogen metabolism through the nitrate reductase (NIT1)/aminomethyl transferase (AMT1)/protein kinase domain-containing protein (A0A2K3CRU5) pathway. These results demonstrate that the nanoparticle morphology can drive divergent toxicity mechanisms in algal cells. Our findings highlight the necessity of incorporating NP morphology into environmental risk assessments and suggest that safer nanomaterial design should consider shape-dependent interactions with aquatic microorganisms.

title: Co-delivery of siPD-L1 and Tat-HSPB1 by G5PBA Enhances the Efficacy of Antitumor Therapy in Clear Cell Renal Cell Carcinoma.
abstract: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) is the most common subtype of renal cell carcinoma and remains challenging to treat at advanced stages due to immune evasion and inefficient intracellular delivery of therapeutic agents. In this study, we synthesized a modified generation 5 (G5) poly(amidoamine) dendrimer (G5PBA) to co-deliver small-interfering RNA targeting programmed death-ligand 1 (siPD-L1) and the antitumor peptide Tat-HSPB1, forming the G5PBA/siPD-L1/Tat-HSPB1 nanocomplex. The agarose gel retardation assay demonstrated that G5PBA efficiently condensed siPD-L1. Furthermore, the peptide encapsulation efficiency and loading capacity were measured, confirming the loading of Tat-HSPB1 into G5PBA/siPD-L1. Flow cytometry showed that G5PBA enhanced the cellular uptake of siPD-L1, while confocal microscopy demonstrated that G5PBA promoted lysosomal escape in Caki-1 cells. Western blot analysis further confirmed that G5PBA effectively reduced the PD-L1 protein expression. In cellular experiments, CCK-8, EdU, and wound-healing assays demonstrated that G5PBA/siPD-L1/Tat-HSPB1 inhibited the viability and migration of ccRCC cells. G5PBA/siPD-L1/Tat-HSPB1 suppressed tumor growth, downregulated PD-L1 expression, enhanced CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell infiltration, and elevated serum levels of IL-2, IL-6, TNF-α, and IFN-γ in mice. Major organs exhibited no obvious histopathological abnormalities upon H&E staining. Serum ALT, AST, and BUN levels showed no significant changes compared with the PBS group, suggesting the preliminary safety profile of G5PBA/siPD-L1/Tat-HSPB1. Collectively, the nanocomplex achieved efficient peptide/siPD-L1 co-delivery and demonstrated significant antitumor activity. This system thus provides a promising strategy and experimental basis for local administration of ccRCC.

title: Brief encounters and lasting impressions-How target protein half-life affects reactive metabolite signaling.
abstract: Cellular stress signaling conveys vital messages to the cell's machinery to respond dynamically to internal and external environmental cues. One prevailing hypothesis for such signaling is to bring about crucial downstream functional changes in the cell's ability to withstand intra- and extra-cellular stress, as exemplified by the NRF2-ARE pathway. Reactive electrophilic metabolites (REMs)-exemplified by the lipid-derived electrophile, 4-hydroxynonenal-are often generated from membrane lipids or respiratory metabolites in inflammatory and stress signaling contexts. REMs harbor an innate ability to irreversibly bind protein-cysteines and form DNA and RNA adducts. Our work has led us to propose a new hypothesis regarding the role of locale-specific REM build-up in stress signaling; whereby, they can label both the majority stable protein residents in a given locale and the minority guests transiently existing within a subcellular compartment at a kinetically significant rate to trigger a 'gain of function' signaling cascade. Much like the NRF2 signaling pathway, such downstream signaling messages could assist the cell's ability to survive against microenvironment-specific stress and adapt on demand. As REMs accumulate in several disease-specific cells, especially age-related disorders such as cancer and neurodegeneration, understanding the functional signal propagation mechanisms shaped by specific REMs engaging with specific biomolecular targets will prove vital for future therapeutic interventions with enhanced precision and context.

title: Cosolvents induce sharp softening and RNA-like twist-stretch coupling of RNA-DNA hybrid.
abstract: Cellular environments generally contain abundant organic cosolvents, yet how in-cell cosolvents modulate the mechanics of RNA-DNA hybrid (RDH) duplex remains unclear. Here, we combined high-precision magnetic tweezer experiments with all-atom molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the structural elasticity of RDH duplexes using PEG200, PEG1000, and ethanol as model cosolvents. We found that high-concentration cosolvents sharply soften RDH duplexes in bending and induce an apparent RNA-like positive twist-stretch coupling. Specifically, for RDH duplex, the bending persistence length P decreases from ∼54 nm to ∼27-35 nm (∼35-50% decrease) by 40% cosolvents. Meanwhile, the twist-stretch coupling parameter dL/dN shifts from ∼0 to -0.56--0.45 nm/turn, approaching that of RNA duplex (∼-0.81 nm/turn). Microscopic analyses revealed that sharp bend softening mainly arises from local hydrogen-bond disruption associated with structural mismatch between RNA and DNA strands and enhanced strand fluctuation driven by increased ion neutralization. Moreover, the RNA-like twist-stretch coupling originates from cosolvent-induced shifts of structure and deformation pathway of RDH duplex toward RNA-like ones from comprehensive analyses at the helix, base-pair, and strand levels. Our findings revealed that cosolvents can substantially reshape the structure and mechanics of RDH duplexes, potentially providing a physical basis for understanding their behavior in cells.

title: Abscopal effect-induced acephalic spermatozoa and testicular dysfunction implicate Cep112 and PI3K/Akt-mTOR signaling.
abstract: The abscopal effect, a systemic phenomenon induced by localized irradiation and associated with inflammatory factor activation, has attracted significant interest in the context of radiotherapy combined with immunotherapy. While recognized as potentially beneficial in oncology, this effect can have detrimental off-target consequences. The underlying mechanisms for abscopal effect-induced testicular dysfunction remain unclear. In this study, we observed a pronounced testicular disruption phenotype characterized by abnormalities in meiosis, blood-testis barrier integrity, and spermatid orientation. Notably, we report the novel finding that the abscopal effect can induce acephalic spermatozoa (headless sperm). Transcriptional analysis by quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction revealed the dysregulation of the expression of centrosomal proteins, known regulators of meiosis and spermiogenesis. By employing RNA interference to knock down centrosomal protein 112 (Cep112), we demonstrated its critical role in spermiogenesis and established its close association with the phosphoinositide 3-kinase/protein kinase B (PI3K/Akt) and mechanistic target of rapamycin/ribosomal protein S6 (mTOR/rpS6) signaling pathways. Our findings indicate that Cep112 mediates cytoskeletal organization in testes and sperm formation via the PI3K/Akt and mTOR/rpS6 pathways, suggesting that Cep112 significantly contributes to abscopal effect-induced spermatogenic dysfunction.

title: Ribosome biogenesis and selective translational control as oncogenic vulnerabilities in hematologic malignancies.
abstract: The translation of the transcriptome into a functional proteome is not a passive readout of mRNA abundance but a primary regulatory layer that actively shapes the oncogenic landscape. In hematologic malignancies, convergent oncogenic signaling pathways, including MYC, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, and tyrosine kinase fusions, directly reprogram the translational apparatus, driving a qualitative shift toward the selective synthesis of pro-survival, proliferative, and stemness-associated proteins. This deregulated program is orchestrated through multiple interconnected axes: the accelerated biogenesis of ribosomes within the nucleolus, the assembly of the eIF4F initiation complex, the activation of stress-adaptive programs like the integrated stress response (ISR), and a sophisticated layer of epitranscriptomic, tRNA, and RNA-binding protein-mediated regulation. Hematologic cancers provide a uniquely informative framework for deconstructing these processes, illustrated by inherited ribosomopathies, such as Diamond-Blackfan anemia syndrome and Shwachman-Diamond syndrome, which resolve the paradox of how ribosomal insufficiency can evolutionarily transition into malignant transformation. Beyond pathogenesis, the translational machinery represents a rich landscape of actionable vulnerabilities. Pharmacological targeting of RNA Polymerase I, eIF4A, and the ISR has demonstrated selective antitumor activity and synergistic potential with established therapies, including BCL-2 inhibition. This review synthesizes mechanistic and clinical evidence to position the ribosome as an active regulatory node rather than a passive decoding machine. We further examine the challenges facing the field, including translational plasticity under therapeutic pressure, the lack of validated companion biomarkers, and the emerging role of translational control in modulating anti-tumor immunity. Ultimately, we argue that defining the disease-specific translational states of leukemia and lymphoma is essential for the next generation of precision oncology, moving beyond genomic landscapes toward a proteomic-centered understanding of malignancy.

title: Metagenomic analysis of oral microbiota in Chinese children with obesity.
abstract: Childhood obesity represents an increasingly severe global public‑health concern, whose precise etiology remains incompletely elucidated and is likely multifactorial. In addition to genetic and lifestyle factors, mounting evidence indicates that the microbes in the digestive tract play a crucial role in the development and progression of obesity. Among them, the oral microbiota may contribute to obesity through mechanisms such as inducing systemic chronic inflammation and promoting gut microbiota dysbiosis. In the present study, saliva samples were collected from 9 obese children and 9 normal-weight children. Using metagenomic sequencing, we aimed to analyze the structural characteristics and functional profiles of the oral microbiota in Chinese school‑age children with obesity, so as to comprehensively dissect the oral microbiome ecology of this population from structural and functional perspectives. The results revealed that the microbiota diversity was similar between the two groups. At the species level, Dialister invisus, Treponema porcinum, Moraxella sp., Moraxella sp. VT 16 12, Moraxella lacunata, and Moraxella caprae were significantly enriched in the normal-weight group. Conversely, Campylobacter concisus, Veillonella sp. oral taxon 158, Veillonella rogosae, Veillonella sp. S13053 19, Streptococcus ilei, and Streptococcus australis were significantly enriched in the obese group. Functional annotation analysis demonstrated significant enrichment of functional genes associated with the hypoxia-inducible factor-1 (HIF-1) signaling pathway, peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor (PPAR) signaling pathway, beta-alanine metabolism, AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) signaling pathway, and apoptosis in the normal-weight group. In contrast, functional genes related to biofilm formation-Vibrio cholerae, selenocompound metabolism, RNA polymerase, xylene degradation, and dioxin degradation were significantly enriched in the obese group. Correlation analysis further revealed strong positive correlations between Veillonella sp. oral taxon 158, Veillonella sp. S13053 19, Streptococcus ilei, Streptococcus australis and the functional pathways of biofilm formation-Vibrio cholerae, selenocompound metabolism, xylene degradation, and dioxin degradation. These observations suggest that the oral microbiome undergoes compositional and functional alterations in children with obesity, implying a potential role of oral microbiota in the etiology of childhood obesity.

title: Intramuscular self-amplifying RNA and adenoviral RSV vaccines program distinct systemic and respiratory mucosal immune architectures.
abstract: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) remains a major cause of severe lower respiratory tract disease in infants, older adults, and immunocompromised individuals, underscoring the need for vaccine strategies that balance systemic protection with frontline respiratory immunity. Although adenoviral and RNA-based RSV are both promising platforms, how the platform itself shapes systemic versus respiratory mucosal immunity under the same antigenic context remains insufficiently defined. We conducted a head-to-head comparison of an LNP-delivered saRNA vaccine (LNP-RSV-preF saRNA) and a recombinant Ad5-vectored vaccine (Ad5-RSV-preF) in mice using intramuscular prime-boost immunization. The two platforms drove distinct immune architectures rather than just differences in response magnitude. LNP-RSV-preF saRNA preferentially promoted respiratory mucosal immunity, including elevated BALF IgG, pulmonary antibody-secreting cells, CD69+ T cells, and lung-resident memory T (TRM) cells, as well as cycling and memory-associated CD8+ T-cell states and durable lung IgA memory. In contrast, Ad5-RSV-preF induced stronger systemic immunity, featured by higher early serum IgG, splenic polyfunctional effector T cells, enhanced germinal center/TFH responses, and effector-polarized CD8 + T cells, with sustained systemic humoral memory. Ad5-vectored and LNP-saRNA vaccine platforms induce distinct compartmentalized immune responses to the same RSV preF antigen. This study establishes a framework for rational platform selection in RSV vaccine design, enabling tailored strategies to balance systemic immunity and respiratory mucosal memory.

title: One protein, many faces: TRAF1 from signaling hub to disease diversity.
abstract: Tumor necrosis factor receptor-associated factor 1 (TRAF1) is a unique member of the TRAF family, distinguished by its lack of an N-terminal RING domain. At the transcriptional level, TRAF1 expression is regulated by diverse mechanisms, including methylation, RNA-binding domain (RBD) proteins, and microRNAs. Post-translationally, TRAF1 undergoes modifications such as M1-linked ubiquitination and phosphorylation. In immune signaling pathways, TRAF1 usually displays functional duality: it activates the canonical NF-κB pathway by enhancing cIAP recruitment downstream of TNFR1, whereas at death domain-lacking TNFR superfamily members (NDDTNFRs), it drives the non-canonical NF-κB pathway through TRAF3 degradation. Conversely, TRAF1 often acts as a negative regulator in Toll-like receptor (TLR) signaling. Within the MAPK pathway, TRAF1 participates in modulating multiple cascades, including ASK1/B-Raf(BRAF)/ERK1. In immune-mediated diseases, TRAF1 contributes to disease pathogenesis by regulating inflammatory cytokines, matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) expression, synovial cell apoptosis and tissue destruction. In infectious diseases, the anti-apoptotic effect of TRAF1 downstream of the 4-1BB signaling pathway serves as a host strategy to combat viral infections by preserving CD8+ T cell survival. However, Helicobacter pylori exploits TRAF1 upregulation to inhibit apoptosis in gastric epithelial cells, facilitating its persistent colonization. This contrast highlights TRAF1's functional diversity across infections. This review summarizes the post-translational regulation of TRAF1, its dual roles in signaling pathways, and its contributions to immune-related and infectious diseases, aiming to clarify its mechanistic complexity within the existing biological framework.

title: Hyperosmotic stress in renal tubular epithelial cells promotes TFEB-dependent autophagy in interstitial fibroblasts by involving extracellular glutamate.
abstract: Renal tubular epithelial-interstitial fibroblast communication maintains kidney homeostasis but promotes disease when dysregulated. Tubular epithelial cells undergo large physiological osmotic fluctuations; however, it remains unclear whether epithelial hyperosmotic stress sends signals to neighboring fibroblasts. Herein, we examined how epithelial hyperosmotic stress regulates fibroblast autophagy and transcription factor EB (TFEB) activity. We used a Transwell co-culture system with rat proximal tubular epithelial cells (NRK-52E) and renal interstitial fibroblasts (NRK-49F), which allowed evaluation of the paracrine effect on fibroblasts mediated by tubular epithelial cells. Hyperosmotic stress in epithelial cells induced the robust nuclear translocation of TFEB in fibroblasts, increased the expression of lysosomal and autophagy-related genes, and enhanced autophagic flux without altering fibroblast viability or proliferation. Although fibroblasts internalized epithelial-derived extracellular vesicles, they did not activate TFEB, suggesting an extracellular vesicles-independent mechanism. RNA sequencing revealed that hyperosmotic stress markedly alters the expression of epithelial solute carrier genes, particularly those encoding amino acid transporters. Analysis of amino acid metabolism revealed corresponding changes in conditioned media, including an increase in extracellular glutamate. Glutamate alone induced TFEB nuclear translocation and autophagy activation in fibroblasts. Both epithelial hyperosmotic co-culture and glutamate treatment activated AMP-activated protein kinase and inhibited mTORC1 signaling, thereby enabling TFEB activation. These results identify extracellular glutamate as a metabolite-based paracrine signal that couples epithelial osmotic stress with TFEB-dependent autophagy in interstitial fibroblasts.
