title: Both Membrane-Bound and Soluble Alkaline Phosphatases Bind Cry1Ca to Potentiate Its Toxicity in Spodoptera litura.
abstract: Membrane-bound alkaline phosphatases (mALPs) are established receptors for several Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) Cry toxins, yet the role of soluble ALPs (sALPs) in the insecticidal mechanism remains unclear. Here, we characterized two midgut-abundant ALPs in Spodoptera litura, SlALP8 and SlALP5, whose expression was down-regulated upon the exposure to Cry1Ca. SlALP8 is a glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchored protein, whereas SlALP5 is secreted. Co-immunoprecipitation assays confirmed that both proteins bind directly to Cry1Ca. RNA interference-mediated knockdown of either SlALP8 or SlALP5 expression increased the larval tolerance to Cry1Ca. Conversely, dietary supplementation with recombinant SlALP8 or SlALP5 protein significantly potentiated the toxicity of Cry1Ca. We demonstrate that membrane-bound SlALP8 acts as a receptor for Cry1Ca and soluble SlALP5 interacts with the toxin to potentiate its toxicity. These findings unveil a coordinated role of mALP and sALP in the Cry toxin efficacy, providing new insight into the mode of action of Cry toxins.

title: Maize 14-3-3 protein ZmGF14-6 interacts with sugarcane mosaic virus HC-Pro and inhibits virus infection.
abstract: Sugarcane mosaic virus, belonging to the genus Potyvirus of the family Potyviridae, is an economically important pathogen infecting maize (Zea mays). Helper component-proteinase (HC-Pro), the potyviral RNA silencing suppressor (RSS), plays crucial roles in countering plants' anti-viral RNA silencing defense mechanisms. 14-3-3 proteins serve as critical regulators in plant response to various stresses. Our previous study had shown that the maize 14-3-3 protein ZmGF14-6 was a potential binding partner of SCMV HC-Pro. In this study, we showed that ZmGF14-6 could interact with SCMV HC-Pro using bimolecular fluorescence complementation, co-immunoprecipitation and luciferase complementation imaging assays. SCMV infection induced ZmGF14-6 expression in maize plants. Knockdown of ZmGF14-6 expression increased susceptibility of maize plants to SCMV infection, while co-expression of ZmGF14-6 inhibited SCMV infection. Furthermore, we revealed that co-expression of ZmGF14-6 led to the degradation of SCMV HC-Pro through the 26S proteasome pathway, thereby diminishing HC-Pro RSS activity. The dimerization of ZmGF14-6 was associated with its binding to HC-Pro and the inhibition of HC-Pro accumulation and SCMV infection. In summary, our findings revealed that the maize 14-3-3 protein ZmGF14-6, which was up-regulated in response to SCMV infection, interacted with HC-Pro to reduce its accumulation, thereby negatively regulating the susceptibility of maize plants to SCMV infection.

title: Chirality and morphology-dependent siRNA delivery for targeted lung cancer therapy with intrinsically chiral gold nanoparticles.
abstract: The clinical translation of RNA interference (RNAi) for lung cancer treatment remains hampered by the lack of delivery vectors that concurrently optimize cellular uptake, target specificity, and in vivo stability. This work reports an intrinsically chiral gold nanoparticle (Au NP) platform with precisely controlled morphology for targeted siRNA delivery. Through a full 2 × 2 factorial design (2 chiralities × 2 morphologies), the work decouples the individual and combined contributions of these two parameters. It is found that right-handed chiral nanoparticles (D-NPs) show significantly faster cellular internalization and higher gene silencing potency than left-handed (L-NPs) and achiral (DL-NPs) counterparts. Beyond chirality, nanoparticle morphology serves as an equally critical parameter: the rhombicuboctahedral (RCO) architecture yields markedly higher silencing efficacy than cubic counterparts with D-chirality. Furthermore, proteomic analysis revealed that Au RCO nanoparticles with different chirality displayed distinct functional enrichment profiles. By D-RCO combination with minimal surface modification, siRNA targeting PD-L1 achieves potent knockdown and robust inhibition of H460 lung cancer proliferation both in vitro and in vivo. This work establishes chirality and morphology as co-designable parameters for gene delivery and provides a mechanistic blueprint for translating chiral nanomaterials into solid tumor therapy.

title: Atorvastatin protects cardiomyocytes from doxorubicin toxicity by modulating YAP/TAZ signaling.
abstract: Doxorubicin (DOX) is a widely used anthracycline chemotherapeutic agent; however, its clinical efficacy is hampered by dose-dependent cardiotoxicity, which can lead to irreversible heart failure. Despite extensive research, effective strategies for preventing or mitigating DOX-induced cardiac injury remain lacking. The Hippo signaling effectors, Yes-associated protein (YAP) and transcriptional co-activator with PDZ-binding motif (TAZ), are known to regulate cardiomyocyte survival, apoptosis, and mitochondrial quality control; however, their role in protecting the heart from DOX toxicity remains unclear. In this study, we investigated whether atorvastatin, a widely prescribed HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor with pleiotropic effects, attenuated DOX-induced cardiomyopathy by modulating the YAP/TAZ signaling axis. In H9c2 cardiomyocytes, DOX suppressed the expression of YAP and TAZ, leading to the downregulation of their downstream targets, Survivin and Park2, and activation of apoptotic cascades. Atorvastatin pretreatment restored YAP/TAZ expression at both mRNA and protein levels and reversed DOX-induced apoptosis. RNA interference-mediated knockdown of YAP or TAZ abolished the protective effects of atorvastatin, confirming the importance of this pathway. In a murine model of DOX cardiotoxicity, atorvastatin preserved left ventricular systolic function, reduced myocardial apoptosis and fibrosis, and restored YAP/TAZ, Survivin, and Park2 expression in the cardiac tissue. These findings suggest that atorvastatin exerts cardioprotective effects by restoring YAP/TAZ-mediated anti-apoptotic and mitochondrial quality control signaling. Our study highlights a novel mechanism via which atorvastatin mitigates DOX-induced cardiotoxicity and supports the therapeutic potential of YAP/TAZ modulation for cardioprotection.

title: Engineered human Argonaute 2 for targeted C-to-U RNA base editing.
abstract: Tools for manipulating RNA that rely on nonhuman proteins, such as ISC-based and Cas-based scaffolds, can lead to unintended and little-understood effects on human cells and present challenges in therapeutic translation. Replacing them with human proteins engineered for expanded, programmable functions could bypass the limitations of these foreign proteins. Here we demonstrate that human Argonaute 2 (AGO2) can be repurposed as a modular RNA targeting domain. AGO2 fused to a C-to-U deaminase enables AGO-led targeted editing of RNA (ALTER). Using guide RNAs that remodel target RNA structure for selective editing and reduced nuclease activity, we show that ALTER achieves, on average, 1.9-fold higher C-to-U editing on mRNA targets in HEK293T cells compared with Cas13 editors CURE and RESCUE. Transcriptome-wide RNA-seq revealed similar or lower levels of off-target editing compared to the same Cas13-based editors. Machine learning models predict that far fewer immunogenic peptides will result from ALTER and we show that ALTER is amenable to a validated workflow for artificial intelligence-directed deimmunization.

title: PFHxS promotes renal fibrosis via PPARγ overactivation-dependent NLRP1 inflammasome-driven pyroptosis.
abstract: Perfluorohexanesulfonic acid (PFHxS) refers to a persistent environmental pollutant associated with declining kidney function. Notably, the underlying mechanisms of PFHxS remain unclear. Here, we demonstrate that chronic PFHxS exposure in mice induces renal fibrosis, as evidenced by collagen deposition, upregulated fibrotic markers, and impaired renal function. Mechanistically, we observed that PFHxS treatment reslulted in increased protein levels of PPARγ and related genes, which further triggered lipid accumulation and mitochondrial ROS production in renal tubular cells. Pharmacological blockade or genetic knockdown of PPARγ markedly ameliorated PFHxS-induced lipid dysregulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and fibrosis. Furthermore, RNA sequencing revealed that PFHxS activated the NLRP1 inflammasome, triggering Caspase-1-dependent pyroptosis, as validated by GSDMD cleavage. Notably, NLRP1 knockdown mitigated PFHxS-induced pyroptosis and fibrotic responses. Collectively, these findings highlight a novel mechanism whereby PFHxS drives renal fibrosis through PPARγ and the subsequent NLRP1 inflammasome-mediated pyroptosis, suggesting PPARγ and NLRP1 as promising therapeutic targets for PFHxS-associated kidney disease.

title: Effect of implant placement on the expression of osteogenic genes in the root of the adjacent tooth: An animal study.
abstract: Dental implants are a common and effective solution for replacing missing teeth. However, the effects of implant placement on adjacent teeth, particularly at the molecular level, remain incompletely understood. Osteogenic genes play a crucial role in bone formation and remodeling, and their expression in the roots of adjacent teeth may be influenced by the presence of dental implants. The aim of the study was to investigate the effect of implant placement on the expression of osteogenic genes, specifically osteopontin (OPN) and osteocalcin (OC), in the root of the adjacent tooth. An experimental study was conducted from January to June 2024 using 20 Wistar rats. Implants were placed adjacent to one of the teeth in each rat, while the contralateral tooth served as the control. Tissue samples were collected from the root of the tooth adjacent to the implant (implant group) and from the corresponding contralateral tooth (control group). RNA was extracted and analyzed using real-time polymerase chain reaction (PCR) to assess the expression levels of the OPN and OC genes. Western blot was performed to evaluate protein expression. The expression of OC was lower in the teeth adjacent to the implants compared with the control group; however, this difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.082). No significant correlation was found between the expression of OC or OPN and the sex of the rats (p > 0.05). Implant placement has a significant influence on the expression of osteogenic genes in the root of the adjacent tooth, particularly by increasing the expression of OC. These findings suggest that dental implants may influence the molecular environment of adjacent teeth, potentially affecting long-term implant success and the health of adjacent teeth. Understanding these molecular changes can help optimize implant procedures and manage potential complications, ultimately improving patient outcomes.

title: ABCC1 Deficiency Mediates Susceptibility to Cd-Induced Hearing Loss via the NOX2/ROS Axis.
abstract: Cadmium (Cd), a prevalent environmental contaminant, is associated with auditory dysfunction. The cochlear blood-labyrinth barrier (BLB) protects the inner ear from toxic substances, a process in which the ATP-binding cassette subfamily C member 1 protein, ABCC1, plays a critical role in expelling toxins from its cells. To understand the specific contribution of ABCC1 to Cd-induced hearing damage, we employed both an in vivo model (ABCC1 knockout mice, Abcc1 -/- mice) and an in vitro endothelial model (ABCC1-deficient human umbilical vein endothelial cells, ABCC1 -/-HUVECs). These models were exposed to CdCl2 to assess auditory responses, histopathology, BLB integrity, and oxidative stress. We also explored the NOX2-ROS/PI3K-AKT pathway using immunofluorescence, Western blotting, and RNA-seq analyses. The results indicate that ABCC1 deficiency exacerbated Cd-induced BLB leakage, promoted spiral ganglion neurons and presynaptic ribbon puncta loss, and increased ABR thresholds. In both animal and cellular models, ABCC1 deficiency enhanced NOX2 expression, ROS accumulation, and AKT dephosphorylation. Significantly, pharmacological inhibition of NOX2 with GSK2795039 attenuated oxidative stress, preserved endothelial barrier function, and partially restored PI3K-AKT signaling. These findings identify ABCC1 as a critical protector of cochlear vascular integrity during Cd exposure, acting through the NOX2-ROS/PI3K-AKT axis, and suggest its potential as a therapeutic target for preventing Cd-induced hearing loss.

title: Reliability and validity of the Turkish translation of the MOS-HIV health survey in people living with HIV.
abstract: Health-related quality of life (HRQoL) is a key patient-centered outcome in HIV care, particularly in the current treatment era in which virological control is increasingly achievable but residual physical, mental, and social burden may persist. However, the clinical applicability of HIV-specific HRQoL instruments in Turkish-speaking people living with HIV (PLWH) remains insufficiently established. We aimed to characterize HRQoL in a multicenter Turkish sample of PLWH and to evaluate whether the Turkish version of the Medical Outcomes Study HIV Health Survey (MOS-HIV) provides reliable and valid scores for use in this population. In this multicenter cross-sectional study, PLWH receiving care at five tertiary training and research hospitals in Istanbul completed the Turkish MOS-HIV. Cognitive debriefing was performed in 20 participants, and 244 were included in the main analysis. Domain and summary scores were calculated according to the user's manual. Internal consistency was assessed in all 244 participants and test-retest reliability in a subsample of 105 after a median of 15 days. Structural validity was examined using domain-level confirmatory factor analysis and known-groups comparisons were conducted according to comorbidity status, CD4 category, history of AIDS-defining illness, and number of tablets in the treatment regimen. Participants had a median age of 37 years and a median CD4 count of 701 cells/mm3; 13.5% had detectable HIV-1 RNA. Floor effects were minimal, whereas ceiling effects were pronounced for role functioning and social functioning and notable for physical functioning and pain. Internal consistency was acceptable across all multi-item domains (Cronbach's α, 0.770-0.924), and test-retest reliability was satisfactory [ICC (2,1), 0.708-0.850]. A parsimonious two-factor domain-level structure was supported. Clinically, comorbidity, CD4 < 500 cells/mm3, and a history of AIDS-defining illness were associated with poorer scores in selected domains, whereas scores did not differ by tablet burden. The Turkish MOS-HIV showed acceptable reliability and structural validity in a young, predominantly male, virologically suppressed population in urban tertiary care, and distinguished HRQoL differences by comorbidity, CD4 status, and history of AIDS-defining illness but not by tablet burden. Evaluation in women, older PLWH and more clinically heterogeneous populations is needed before broader use.

title: Iron homeostasis landscape informs patient survival and neoadjuvant chemotherapy response in cancer.
abstract: Cancer cells frequently alter iron metabolism by increasing uptake or decreasing export, promoting oncogenesis and proliferation. However, the quantitative relationship between iron homeostasis and cancer remains underexplored. We simplified these alterations into measurable changes in the expression levels of iron transport-related genes. We investigated the expression of iron transport-related genes by comparing genomic data of 478 human cancer cell lines to 105 normal tissue samples, as well as analyzing clinically paired 6903 tumor to 709 normal samples. We revealed that cancer cells exhibited increased expression of transferrin receptor 1 (TFR1) or CD44 for iron uptake and decreased expression of ferroportin for iron efflux to favor iron accumulation. Using machine learning, we identified TFR1, CD44, and ferroportin as the top three features consistently associated most with patient survival. We developed a cancer-specific iron risk score (CIRS) using parametric time-to-event models based on RNA-seq data from TFR1, CD44, and ferroportin in 4723 patients spanning 15 cancers. The CIRS, cross-validated in five external datasets, significantly stratified survival risk for various cancers, and predicted chemotherapy response in two independent breast cancer pharmacogenomic datasets. Our study enhances the understanding of the relationship between iron homeostasis, survival, and chemotherapy response, laying the groundwork for iron-targeted therapies.

title: De novo variants in the essential splicing factor gene SRSF3 cause variable developmental phenotypes.
abstract: SRSF3 (SRp20), a member of the serine/arginine-rich protein family of splicing factors, plays a central role in constitutive and alternative splicing. The C-terminal arginine/serine-rich domain of SRSF3 undergoes dynamic phosphorylation cycles that regulate its subcellular localization, protein-protein interactions, and nuclear mRNA export while also indirectly modulating the RNA-binding capability. We report nine individuals with variable developmental phenotypes, including developmental delay and/or mild to moderate intellectual disability as the most consistent feature, and de novo SRSF3 variants. These variants comprise c.181G>C (p.Asp61His) and c.242C>G (p.Ser81Trp), affecting highly conserved residues within the RNA recognition motif, c.330_331del (p.Pro111Serfs∗20), c.402_403del (p.Arg137Ilefs∗16), c.477dup (p.Ser160Valfs∗3), and a recurrent nonsense variant c.445C>T (p.Arg149∗). For c.330_331del, nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) was predicted. Qualitative RT-PCR followed by Sanger sequencing and RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) of fibroblasts from this individual demonstrated NMD of SRSF3 transcripts containing the variant. However, overall SRSF3 mRNA and protein levels were comparable to control cells, suggestive of a compensatory mechanism acting in these cells. Comprehensive functional studies of ectopically expressed SRSF3Asp61His, SRSF3Ser81Trp, SRSF3Arg137Ilefs∗16, SRSF3Arg149∗, and SRSF3Ser160Valfs∗3 in HEK293T cells revealed reduced complex formation with polyadenylated RNA as well as intrinsic instability of C-terminally truncated variant proteins, correlating with decreased C-terminal phosphorylation. Complex formation with the nuclear export proteins YTHDC1 and NXF1 was reduced for SRSF3Arg137Ilefs∗16 and SRSF3Arg149∗ and increased for SRSF3Ser81Trp. Additionally, nucleocytoplasmic shuttling, assessed in HeLa cells, was reduced for the C-terminally truncated SRSF3 variant proteins. Together, our data demonstrate distinct functional defects for the disease-associated SRSF3 variants, which may underlie phenotypic variability in affected individuals.

title: Schrödinger-Bass Bridge Barycenter Models for Measure-Valued Data
abstract: Barycenter models, based on stochastic and deterministic optimal transport bridges between probability measures, have proven to be useful for supervised and unsupervised learning for (probability) measure-valued data. In this paper, we utilize the directional asymmetry and dual drift-diffusion control arising in the recently proposed Schrödinger-Bass Bridge (SBB) between two measures, and propose \textit{SBB-encoder}, \textit{SBB-decoder}, \textit{SBB-symmetric}, and \textit{SBB-Markovian} barycenter models. For each of these novel models, our first theoretical result establishes the existence of the SBB-barycenter under mild assumptions. Our second theoretical result characterizes the decoder SBB-barycenter of Gaussians where we show that for Gaussian input measures, the decoder formulation admits a Gaussian minimizer, reducing barycenter computation to a finite-dimensional optimization and yielding a compact algorithm. For general input measures, we derive a hybrid Wasserstein gradient particle descent scheme for all four formulations using the SBB dual representation. Finally, we utilize these algorithms for solving distributional-inverse/interpolation problems arising in the context of spatial images and single-cell RNA sequencing data, where we show that the SBB-decoder and Markovian barycenter allow us to interpolate between successive time points. Results show that our method outperforms existing barycenter models for measure interpolation and inference.

title: CIRP: New Horizons for CNS Injury Biomarkers and Therapy.
abstract: Cold-inducible RNA-binding protein (CIRP) is a stress-response protein that protects cells under conditions of low temperature and other stresses. The expression of CIRP is induced by various stressors. CIRP regulates gene expression through complex, multi-layered mechanisms and plays a central role in physiological and pathological processes, including cell proliferation, apoptosis, inflammatory responses, and circadian rhythms. In central nervous system (CNS) injuries, CIRP exhibits a dual role. Intracellular CIRP has a neuroprotective function. In contrast, when released into the extracellular space as eCIRP, it acts as a damage-associated molecular pattern (DAMP) that exacerbates neuroinflammation. Serum levels of eCIRP are significantly elevated in patients with CNS injuries, such as acute ischemic stroke and intracerebral hemorrhage, suggesting its potential as a biomarker for diagnosis and prognosis. Furthermore, targeting the eCIRP signaling pathway has shown significant therapeutic effects in various models of neurological injury. Strategies include using inhibitory peptides like C23 and M3, as well as microRNA-based approaches. Here, we systematically review the molecular characteristics, expression regulation, and biological functions of CIRP, with a focus on its neuroprotective role, biomarker potential, and therapeutic targeting in CNS injuries.

title: hMPV M2-2 protein modulates host mRNA alternative splicing to favor virus replication.
abstract: Human metapneumovirus (hMPV) is a widespread and prevalent respiratory pathogen, yet the mechanisms by which hMPV modulates host gene expression to facilitate replication remain incompletely characterized. Here, we systematically profiled hMPV-host protein-protein interactions by affinity purification-mass spectrometry and assessed their impact on host messenger RNA (mRNA) splicing using RNA sequencing, complemented by genetic perturbation, protein interaction assays, and fluorescence microscopy-based subcellular localization and colocalization analyses. Among the viral proteins analyzed, the regulatory protein M2-2 was found to directly interact with multiple splicing factors. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that M2-2 triggers extensive changes in alternative splicing across host genes, notably affecting genes encoding serine-threonine kinase receptor-associated protein (STRAP) and tetratricopeptide repeat, ankyrin repeat and coiled-coil containing 2 (TANC2), both of which exhibit distinct splicing patterns during hMPV infection. Knockdown of M2-2 using short hairpin RNA (shRNA) during hMPV infection reversed M2-2-driven changes in the splicing patterns of STRAP and TANC2, confirming its regulatory role. Functional knockout of STRAP or TANC2 significantly impaired viral replication, indicating that the M2-2-favored isoforms are required for efficient viral propagation. Collectively, our findings demonstrate a novel mechanism by which hMPV M2-2 hijacks the host splicing machinery to reprogram key factors that facilitate viral replication. This extends the functional repertoire of M2-2 and highlights the virus-spliceosome interface as a potential therapeutic target for anti-hMPV intervention.

title: NAT10-mediated ac4C modification of BMP6 regulates osteogenic differentiation of bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cells in the pathogenesis of Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis.
abstract: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) is a three-dimensional spinal deformity. Bone morphogenetic protein 6 (BMP6) drives osteogenesis; this study probes BMP6 mechanism and its potential role in the impaired osteogenic differentiation of AIS-BMSCs. AIS-BMSCs were isolated and their surface markers (CD34, CD45, CD90, and CD105) were analyzed by flow cytometry. Osteogenic differentiation was assessed through alizarin red S staining quantification and ALP activity assays, while the expression of osteogenic markers osteocalcin (OCN), runt-related transcription factor 2 (RUNX2), BMP6, N-acetyltransferase 10 (NAT10), and Smad1/5/9 signaling pathway was detected by Western blot. The transcriptional and protein levels of BMP6 and NAT10, as well as knockdown and overexpression efficiencies, were measured by qPCR and Western blot. Cell viability was determined using the CCK-8 assay. Potential N4-acetylcytidine (ac4C) modification sites in BMP6 were predicted using the PACES webserver. The interaction between NAT10 and BMP6 was examined by RNA immunoprecipitation (RIP) and luciferase reporter assays. Rescue assays confirmed NAT10 pro-osteo effect requires BMP6. AIS-BMSCs showed reduced ALP activity, mineralization capacity, and RUNX2/OCN expression, along with downregulated BMP6 expression; BMP6 re-expression rescued these deficits in vitro. NAT10 mediates ac4C acetylation of BMP6 mRNA, extending its half-life and boosting osteogenesis, whereas inhibition of NAT10 or ac4C modification reversed these effects. BMP6 knockdown abolished NAT10-enhanced mineralization and p-Smad1/5/9, indicating that NAT10 acts via BMP6-Smad1/5/9. NAT10-mediated ac4C modification stabilizes BMP6 mRNA, activates Smad1/5/9, and ameliorates the impaired osteogenic differentiation of AIS-BMSCs in vitro. These findings suggest a potential mechanism by which NAT10-BMP6 signaling may influence osteogenesis in AIS, but they are based solely on in vitro experiments.

title: HEXB as a Candidate Target Gene in Keloid Radiotherapy: Based on Multi-Omics Analysis and Mendelian Randomization.
abstract: Keloid is a common and treatment-refractory conditions in plastic surgery and dermatology. Although radiotherapy for keloid has attracted increasing attention in recent years, its mechanism at the genetic level remains poorly characterized. This study investigated the relationship between radiation-related genes (RRGs) and keloid through an integrated multi-omics and machine learning framework, and to explore potential therapeutic agents targeting the identified key gene. Single-cell RNA sequencing and multiple Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) datasets were integrated to investigate the association between RRGs and keloid. Multiple machine learning algorithms were applied to assess potential causal relationships, followed by Mendelian randomization (MR) analysis to investigate potential relationships. Spatial transcriptomics was employed to localize gene expression within keloid tissue, and virtual knockout analysis was performed to assess the functional role of the candidate gene in tissue architecture. Finally, molecular docking was conducted to screen potential therapeutic agents targeting HEXB, and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were performed to evaluate the stability of the resulting protein-ligand complexes. Hexosaminidase Subunit Beta (HEXB) was identified as a key gene. MR analysis further provided genetic evidence supporting a potential protective association between HEXB and keloid, identifying HEXB as a candidate protective gene. Spatial transcriptomics localized HEXB to the fibrotic dermal matrix with intralesional heterogeneity, while virtual knockout analysis implicated HEXB in maintaining epidermal-mesenchymal boundary integrity. Molecular docking demonstrated that HEXB predicted binding to several drugs, such as tamoxifen and estramustine, suggesting that HEXB may serve as a key target of these agents in keloid treatment. This study identifies HEXB as a candidate protective gene in keloid through an integrated multi-omics approach and suggests that HEXB may serve as a molecular target for potential therapeutic agents. These findings provide new directions for understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying radiotherapy in keloid and for developing targeted therapeutic strategies.

title: Berberine alleviates radiation-induced lung injury by promoting microbiota-derived inosine via the gut-lung axis.
abstract: Radiation-induced lung injury (RILI) is a common complication of radiotherapy. Although berberine (BBR) has been suggested to be associated with reduced RILI incidence, the underlying mechanisms remain unknown. Here, we investigated whether the gut microbiota mediates the radioprotective effects of BBR using a C57BL/6 RILI mouse model with 20 Gy thoracic irradiation (n = 6 per group). BBR (100 mg/kg) and inosine (INO, 300 mg/kg) were administered orally in vivo. Antibiotic depletion and fecal microbiota transplantation were performed to assess microbiota dependence. Lung injury was assessed by histology, pulmonary function, and cytokine levels. Gut microbiota was analyzed by 16S rRNA sequencing, and metabolites were profiled using LC-MS/MS. Transcriptomic and epigenomic alterations were assessed by RNA sequencing, ATAC sequencing, and CUT&Tag analysis. Molecular docking and surface plasmon resonance were used to assess metabolite-protein interactions. We demonstrated that BBR alleviated RILI in a microbiota-dependent manner. BBR increased Akkermansia muciniphila abundance and metabolite INO levels. Mechanistically, INO was associated with reduced neuron navigator 3 (NAV3) expression, accompanied by decreased chromatin accessibility and increased histone H3 lysine 27 trimethylation (H3K27me3) at the NAV3 locus. Together, these findings reveal a gut microbiota-mediated mechanism underlying BBR-mediated protection against RILI, and suggest microbiota-informed biomarkers for risk stratification.

title: Exploring the mechanisms of baicalein in lung adenocarcinoma: an integrative preliminary study with focused experimental assessment in A549 cells.
abstract: Lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) continues to present therapeutic challenges because of pathway redundancy and treatment resistance, underscoring the need for multi-target and systems-level strategies. Baicalein (BA), a flavonoid metabolite from Scutellaria baicalensis Georgi, shows antitumor potential, yet integrative and immune-related evaluations of BA in LUAD remain limited. We integrated network analyses with TCGA-LUAD transcriptomics, weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA), network topology, GO/KEGG enrichment, bulk RNA-seq-based immune-infiltration estimation (CIBERSORT), molecular docking, and clinical association analysis (GEPIA2/HPA). Cell viability was assessed in A549 cells​ using the CCK-8 assay, and AKT1 phosphorylation and BCL2 protein expression were further examined experimentally by western blot analysis. A total of 117 candidate BA-LUAD overlapping targets were identified, and six candidate hub genes (EGFR, AKT1, TP53, BCL2, HIF1A, and ESR1) were prioritized. Enrichment analyses suggested that the candidate network was associated with oncogenic signaling and stress-response programs, particularly PI3K-AKT/MAPK signaling, ROS-related processes, apoptosis, and p53 signaling. CCK-8 assays showed that BA reduced A549 cell viability in vitro, with IC50 values of 54.93 μM at 24 h and 22.83 μM at 48 h. Among the prioritized candidates, AKT1 and BCL2 were selected for focused experimental assessment in A549 cells. BA treatment reduced AKT1 phosphorylation and BCL2 protein expression in A549 cells, whereas total AKT1 remained largely unchanged. HIF1A expression showed broad associations with computationally estimated immune-cell fractions and poorer overall survival. These findings prioritize a BA-associated candidate network in LUAD involving kinase signaling, apoptosis-related regulation, oxidative-stress responses, and immune-microenvironment associations. The CCK-8 results support an inhibitory effect of BA on A549 cell viability in vitro, and the observed changes in AKT1 phosphorylation and BCL2 protein expression provide focused experimental support for selected components of the candidate network; further in vitro and in vivo studies are required to validate biological relevance and translational potential.

title: Targeting neuronal FKBP5 attenuates mechanical allodynia by suppressing NF-κB-mediated neuroinflammation in an NTG-induced chronic migraine mouse model.
abstract: Chronic migraine (CM) is a debilitating neurological disorder characterized by persistent trigeminovascular sensitization and neuroinflammation. While FK506-binding protein 51 (FKBP5) modulates spinal neuroinflammation in chronic pain, its specific role in trigeminovascular nociceptive processing and CM pathogenesis remains largely unknown. We used a nitroglycerin (NTG)-induced CM mouse model. Following RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) of total RNA isolated from trigeminal nucleus caudalis (TNC) tissue lysates, target expression was validated via reverse transcription quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR), Western blotting, and immunofluorescence. To establish causality, we used a neuron-specific CRISPR-Cas9 editing system for Fkbp5 knockout within the TNC, alongside pharmacological interventions using the specific FKBP5 antagonist SAFit2 and the nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) inhibitor PDTC. Migraine-like behaviors were evaluated using von Frey filaments, coupled with biochemical analyses of NF-κB cascade activation and trigeminovascular neuroinflammation. RNA-seq, RT-qPCR, Western blotting, and immunofluorescence consistently confirmed a marked upregulation of Fkbp5 mRNA and FKBP5 protein in the TNC of NTG-treated mice, predominantly localized to neurons. Concurrently, significant microglial and astrocytic activation was observed in the TNC. Both neuron-specific Fkbp5 knockout and pharmacological inhibition with SAFit2 significantly attenuated NTG-induced periorbital and hind paw mechanical allodynia. Furthermore, FKBP5 deficiency blunted the NTG-triggered phosphorylation of p65 and IκBα, effectively suppressing the downstream release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including interleukin-1β (IL-1β), interleukin-6 (IL-6), and tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), as well as the upregulation of calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) and c-Fos. Crucially, targeted blockade of the NF-κB cascade with PDTC recapitulated the protective behavioral and biochemical effects of FKBP5 deficiency. We demonstrate that neuronal FKBP5 is significantly associated with CM pathogenesis. FKBP5 sustains mechanical allodynia by activating the NF-κB-mediated neuroinflammatory cascade. Consequently, targeting FKBP5 represents a promising therapeutic strategy for CM.

title: Targeting androgen receptor as a novel radiosensitizing therapy to improve long-term survival and anti-tumor immunity in glioblastoma via TGF-β/Smad3 Axis reprogramming.
abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) remains the most aggressive primary adult brain cancer with limited therapeutic options. Our prior research demonstrated that androgen receptor antagonists (ARAs) enhance survival in GBM mouse models by preferentially suppressing glioma stem cells. This study investigates the potential of ARAs as radiosensitizers in combination with radiotherapy (RT). Combined effects of ARAs and RT were evaluated using an orthotopic GBM mouse model. RNA-Seq and TCGA analyses delineated AR-associated regulatory networks, while integrated cellular and molecular approaches utilizing human and mouse GBM cell lines, as well as in patient-derived primary high-grade glioma cultures, interrogated signaling and immune paradigms. ARA treatment induced G2/M cell cycle arrest, apoptosis, and downregulated DNA repair genes, with AR expression correlating with the DNA repair and TGF-β pathway. In both immortalized GBM cell lines and primary high-grade glioma cultured cells, ARAs in combination with RT showed only a modest enhancement of radiosensitivity. However, in an orthotopic GBM mouse model, ARA + RT demonstrated a strong synergy, achieving 100% long-term survival, compared to less than 50% with ARA alone and 0% with RT alone. Mechanistically, ARA modulated the TGF-β pathway, durably switching from Smad3 linker to c-terminal phosphorylation (pSmad3C) and inhibiting the LIF/STAT3 axis. Distinct TGF-βs ligand expression patterns were observed in ARA-treated GBM cells. A protein-protein interaction noted between AR and pSmad3, which was disrupted following ARA treatment, leading to elevated protein levels and nuclear localization of pSmad3C (S423/425), indicating normalization/activation of the TGF-β/pSmad3C-dependent anti-tumorigenic cascade. Comprehensive analyses in GBM cell lines and mouse model tissues demonstrated pathway reprogramming characterized by elevated TGF-β2 and increased pSmad3C. Rescue experiments using a TGFβRII degrader with ARA abolished pSmad3C phosphorylation, confirming the functional significance of TGFβRII/pSmad3C axis. Tissue analysis revealed immune activation in the tumor microenvironment, while peripheral blood and spleen showed systemic immune responses following ARA + RT. Our study provides novel insights into how ARAs enhance RT efficacy through immunomodulation involving TGF-β/pSmad3C cascade, offering therapeutic implications in GBM.

title: Biomaterial characteristics and biofluid composition differentially modulate protein adsorption and macrophage phenotype on common surgical polymers with proteome-transcriptome concordance.
abstract: Dysregulated macrophage responses to common surgical polymers contribute to implantable medical device failure. While biomaterial characteristics are known to influence macrophage behavior, the contribution of the local biological milieu and the adsorbed proteins remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate how biomaterial physicochemical properties and biofluid composition differentially modulate adsorbed proteomes and macrophage transcriptomes on common surgical polymers as well as explore the link between the latter two. We first quantify the stiffness, roughness, wettability and protein adsorption capacity of PDMS, PP, PTFE, HDPE and nylon, and characterize the protein composition of plasma, serum and surgical drain fluid obtained from breast reconstruction patients. Then, we expose these common surgical polymers to the three clinically-relevant biofluids and profile the resulting adsorbed proteomes with liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS). In parallel, we culture THP-1 macrophages on the same preconditioned biomaterials and analyze their transcriptomes using RNA sequencing. We find that biofluid composition primarily establishes the adsorbed proteomes which the biomaterials subsequently refine into material-specific protein signatures. In contrast, biomaterial characteristics, except protein adsorption capacity, primarily determine macrophage transcriptomes, with stiffness, roughness and hydrophobicity being associated with inflammation, metabolic stress and tissue remodeling programs. Proteome-transcriptome integration reveals strong global concordance, alongside a subset of proteins - particularly lipoproteins and metabolism-associated proteins (e.g., zinc-alpha-2-macroglobulin and transthyretin) - that appears to disproportionally drive this relationship. Together, these findings support a model in which common surgical polymers regulate macrophage responses via both direct physicochemical cues and indirect protein-mediated mechanisms. STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE: Implantable medical devices fail because protein adsorption onto their biomaterial surfaces initiates the foreign body response, culminating in inflammation and fibrotic encapsulation. How the composition of the adsorbed protein layer shapes macrophage behavior and subsequent inflammation remains largely unknown. Moreover, the relative contributions of biomaterial properties and the surrounding fluid has not been clearly defined. Integrating proteomics and transcriptomics, we demonstrate that biofluid composition establishes the structure of the adsorbed protein layer, whereas biomaterial properties refine it into protein signatures that are concordant with corresponding macrophage transcriptomes. Notably, lipid handling and metabolism-associated proteins emerge as potential predictors of inflammatory, metabolic stress and tissue-remodeling macrophage responses. These findings establish protein adsorption as a critical design consideration in engineering more biocompatible biomaterials.

title: Rab7a promotes the progression of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma via the Hippo signaling pathway.
abstract: Ras-related protein Rab7a participates in fundamental cancer cell processes; however, its role in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) remains unclear. In this study, we aimed to define Rab7a's oncogenic functions in ESCC and its involvement in the Hippo signaling pathway. Rab7a expression was assessed using ESCC datasets and validated by immunohistochemical analysis of ESCC tissues. We examined functional effects using small interfering RNA knockdown and Yes-associated protein 1 (YAP1) overexpression rescue experiments, primarily by evaluating proliferation, migration, invasion, and apoptosis in ESCC TE-1 cells. We also established a xenograft model for in vivo validation. Regarding its mechanism(s) of action, we analyzed the effects of Rab7a on Hippo core kinases (LATS1/2 and MOB1) and further assessed YAP nuclear localization in ESCC cells. Rab7a was overexpressed in ESCC tissues, and elevated expression correlated with aggressive clinicopathological features, including advanced tumor, node, metastasis stage, positive lymph node metastasis, deep tumor invasion, and poor differentiation. Rab7a knockdown suppressed cellular proliferation, migration, and invasion and induced apoptosis in vitro while inhibiting tumor growth and decreasing Ki-67 expression in vivo. Mechanistically, Rab7a silencing downregulated YAP1, p-YAP1, CTGF, and survivin without affecting MST1. Furthermore, Rab7a knockdown significantly increased p-LATS1/2 levels without altering total LATS1/2 or MOB1 expression and decreased YAP nuclear accumulation. Importantly, YAP1 overexpression effectively reversed the suppressive effects of Rab7a knockdown on malignant phenotypes at both the functional and molecular levels, and restored the expression of downstream targets. Rab7a depletion also reversed an epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT)-like phenotype, as evidenced by upregulated E-cadherin and downregulated vimentin and Snail. This effect was rescued by YAP1 overexpression. Our findings demonstrate that Rab7a promotes ESCC progression by regulating the Hippo pathway effector YAP, thus inducing an EMT-like phenotype. Rab7a may serve as a promising prognostic biomarker and therapeutic target in ESCC that functions upstream of LATS1/2 to modulate YAP-mediated tumor progression.

title: Single-cell RNA sequencing profiles age-related transcriptional landscapes in human hair follicle cells.
abstract: Hair loss and graying, the earliest visible signs of skin aging, are driven by the functional decline of hair follicle stem cells and their niches. To elucidate the transcriptional mechanisms involved in scalp aging, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of human scalp samples using single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomic technologies. Our study profiled the transcriptomes of 57,181 cells from scalp samples obtained from four young, six middle-aged, and one elderly individual. The integrated bioinformatic pipeline included cell clustering, spatial deconvolution, pseudotime trajectory, as well as cell-type specific gene expression, and intercellular communication analysis. An additional 92 volunteers were included, comprising 90 (37 young, 27 middle-aged, and 26 elderly) for trichoscopic examination, one young individual for senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-gal) staining, and one elderly individual for both MKI67 immunofluorescence and SA-β-gal staining. This approach led to several key findings: we identified three subtypes of mitotic keratinocytes that localized in the interfollicular epidermis (IFE), outer root sheath (ORS), and hair matrix, with pseudotime trajectory further confirming their transitional stage. Furthermore, in middle-aged scalps, we observed activated activator protein 1 (AP-1) transcription factor complex in keratinocytes, upregulated DCT gene in melanocytes, and decreased bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) and noncanonical wingless/integrated (ncWNT) signaling in dermal papilla (DP)-keratinocytes cross-talk. Due to the insufficient sample size and under-representation of elderly samples, transcriptional features associated with late aging, sex, and scalp regions were not completely captured. Nevertheless, our study provides valuable cell-resolved transcriptional insights into hair follicle aging and may support the development of future regenerative therapies.

title: Integrative microbiome and transcriptome analyses identify parity-associated alterations in rectal fecal microbiota and peripheral immune transcriptional signatures in dairy cows.
abstract: Increasing parity in dairy cows is accompanied by cumulative physiological, reproductive, lactational, and management exposures that may coincide with changes in metabolic and immune status. However, the relationships among parity group, distal hindgut microbial communities, peripheral immune-related transcription, and their coordinated variation remain incompletely understood. In this cross-sectional observational study, 40 nonpregnant Holstein cows in mid-lactation without recorded disease were randomly selected from an eligible population within a commercial dairy herd and classified into naturally occurring parity groups: primiparous cows (PrC; parity = 1; n = 20) and multiparous cows (MuC; parities = 2-5; n = 20). Rectal fecal 16S ribosomal RNA (16S rRNA) gene sequencing and peripheral whole-blood RNA sequencing were integrated to characterize microbial and immune-related transcriptional differences between the two groups. Multiparous cows had lower Shannon diversity, Chao1 richness, and observed amplicon sequence variant (ASV) richness than primiparous cows, but a higher Simpson dominance index (D), consistently indicating lower α-diversity and greater community dominance in multiparous cows. A one-factor permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) based on Bray-Curtis distances indicated that parity-group membership was associated with a modest proportion of the variation in rectal fecal microbial composition (R² = 0.0581, permutation p = 0.004). Using linear discriminant analysis effect size (LEfSe), random forest, and analysis of compositions of microbiomes with bias correction 2 (ANCOM-BC2), 13 candidate genera were identified by at least two analytical approaches. Prevotellaceae_UCG-003 was more abundant in PrC, whereas Turicibacter, Clostridium_sensu_stricto_1, Acetitomaculum, and Lachnospiraceae_NK3A20_group were more abundant in MuC. Phylogenetic Investigation of Communities by Reconstruction of Unobserved States 2 (PICRUSt2)-based inference indicated group differences in predicted functional potential related to protein synthesis, amino acid and carbohydrate metabolism, bacterial motility, chemotaxis, and signal transduction; these results represent predicted rather than directly measured microbial functions. Whole-blood RNA sequencing identified 189 differentially expressed genes in the comparison between MuC and PrC, including 116 genes with higher transcript abundance in MuC and 73 with higher transcript abundance in PrC. Overall KEGG analysis of the complete DEG set identified 38 significantly enriched pathways, many of which were related to immune and inflammatory processes. Direction-stratified KEGG analysis further indicated that broad significant immune-related enrichment was mainly associated with genes showing higher transcript abundance in PrC cows, whereas only one KEGG term remained significantly enriched among the MuC-higher genes after Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Integration of differential expression, weighted gene co-expression network analysis, and protein-protein interaction analysis prioritized matrix metallopeptidase 9 (MMP9), mitogen-activated protein kinase 13 (MAPK13), and WD repeat domain, phosphoinositide interacting 1 (WIPI1) as candidate hub genes, all of which showed higher transcript abundance in MuC. Sparse partial least squares integration further identified a multivariate association structure involving selected candidate fecal genera and immune-related genes. This study provides exploratory multi-omics evidence of differences in rectal fecal microbial composition, predicted microbial functional potential, and peripheral blood immune-related transcription between primiparous and multiparous cows. The coordinated microbiome-transcriptome patterns identify candidate microbial and transcriptional features for future investigation. Because this was a cross-sectional observational study, the findings should be interpreted as associations rather than causal effects of parity. Longitudinal studies and validation in independent herds are required.

title: FLASH effect on the liver and spleen of mice-a transcriptional perspective.
abstract: FLASH radiotherapy (FLASH-RT), delivered at an ultra-high dose rate (typically ≥ 40 Gy/s), has been shown to reduce normal tissue toxicity compared with conventional dose-rate radiotherapy (CONV-RT). However, the transcriptomic mechanisms underlying FLASH-mediated protection remain incompletely understood. This study aimed to compare the biological effects of FLASH and CONV irradiation on mouse liver and spleen tissues and to identify molecular pathways associated with the FLASH effect from a transcriptional perspective. C57BL/6J male mice received a single 12 Gy abdominal dose delivered at either 2 Gy/min (CONV) or 100 Gy/s (FLASH). Twelve days after irradiation, spleen and liver tissues were harvested for histological section analysis and RNA-seq. Inflammatory responses in the spleen and liver were assessed by hematoxylin-eosin staining (H&E staining) and immunohistochemical quantification. A series of bioinformatic analyses, such as gene enrichment, protein-protein interaction (PPI) analysis, and transcription factor prediction, were performed to explore the effect of FLASH irradiation. Subsequently, reverse transcription quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR), western blot analysis, and immunohistochemical quantification were used to verify the bioinformatic results. Histological and immunohistochemical analyses showed less prominent inflammatory changes and lower immune-cell marker staining in mouse spleen and liver after FLASH than after CONV irradiation at 12 days post-irradiation. Bioinformatic analysis and corresponding experimental results revealed that compared to CONV irradiation, FLASH irradiation induced down-regulation of oxidative phosphorylation and cytoplasmic translation pathways in both mouse liver and spleen. Meanwhile, immune-related pathways, especially interferon β (IFNβ) signaling pathways, were significantly activated in both tissues after FLASH than after CONV irradiation. For these three pathways, key transcription factors were further identified and verified. Notably, STAT1 was found to play a potentially critical role in the upregulation of the IFNβ-related pathway under FLASH irradiation conditions in both liver and spleen. FLASH irradiation induces distinct metabolic and immune adaptations in normal mouse liver and spleen tissues compared with CONV irradiation. The coordinated suppression of metabolic and translational pathways, together with activation of IFNβ-STAT1 signaling program, provides transcriptomic evidence for potential mechanisms underlying FLASH-mediated normal tissue sparing. These findings offer candidate pathways and molecular markers for future functional validation and support the clinical translation of FLASH-RT.

title: Key genes and pathways of pulmonary hypertension identified by integrating bulk and single-cell RNA sequencing.
abstract: Pulmonary hypertension (PH) is a progressive vascular disease, yet the underlying cell-type-specific molecular networks and diagnostic biomarkers remain incompletely defined. Integrating single-cell and bulk transcriptomics, we identified 14 pulmonary cell types in PH, with smooth muscle cells (SMCs) as a central communication hub interacting with monocytes and macrophages. High-dimensional weighted gene co-expression network analysis (hdWGCNA) revealed 4 SMC modules enriched in extracellular matrix organization, TGF-β, and HIF-1 pathways. A five-gene diagnostic signature distinguished PH from controls with an area under the curve of 0.895. Immune infiltration and enrichment analysis showed that activated CD4 memory T cells, activated dendritic cells, and resting mast cells increased in the PH group, while angiogenesis and epithelial-mesenchymal transition pathway were upregulated. In hypoxic human pulmonary artery SMCs, milk fat globule-epidermal growth factor-8 (MFGE8), secreted frizzled-related protein 2 (SFRP2), S100 calcium-binding protein A11 (S100A11), and procollagen C-endopeptidase enhancer 2 (PCOLCE2) were upregulated, and their knockdown suppressed proliferation, highlighting them as potential biomarkers and drivers of vascular remodeling, revealing a new molecular mechanism for PH and providing insights for potential therapeutic targets.

title: Variant-informed multimodal tissue-state modeling reveals an NRF2 stress niche and dependency axis in KEAP1/NFE2L2-altered cancer.
abstract: Cancer genotypes influence transcriptional programs, spatial organization, histopathology, and treatment-response states, yet these molecular and tissue-level features are often analyzed separately in public-data studies. VISTA was developed as a variant-informed, multimodal framework for modeling genotype-linked tissue states and prioritizing validation-ready biological hypotheses. VISTA integrates somatic variants, protein-region and AlphaMissense-informed priors, RNA-state scoring, whole-slide image embeddings, immunotherapy cohorts, spatial and single-cell references, cell-line dependency maps, and pharmacogenomic screens. We evaluated the framework in KEAP1/NFE2L2-altered lung cancer and melanoma, using the NRF2 stress axis as a biologically defined test case. Analyses incorporated project-adjusted modeling, bootstrap confidence intervals, permutation testing, leave-project sensitivity analyses, independent tumor-level validation cohorts, fixed-effect external meta-analysis, model-system analyses using DepMap/CCLE, tissue-context analyses, immunotherapy cohorts, and exploratory whole-slide image analyses. In TCGA LUAD, LUSC, and SKCM pilot cohorts, KEAP1 and NFE2L2 alterations were consistently associated with NRF2 stress activation across project-adjusted models and sensitivity analyses. Independent analyses of CPTAC LUAD, CPTAC LSCC, and non-TCGA LUAD cohorts reproduced higher NRF2-state scores in KEAP1/NFE2L2-altered tumors. Fixed-effect external meta-analysis supported associations with both KEAP1 mutation and combined KEAP1-or-NFE2L2 alteration status. DepMap/CCLE analyses provided complementary model-system evidence: KEAP1/NFE2L2-mutant models had higher NRF2 scores, while NRF2-high or KEAP1/NFE2L2-mutant contexts showed stronger NFE2L2 dependency. Tissue-context analyses positioned NRF2 stress near hypoxic, stromal, myeloid, and immune programs. Immunotherapy cohorts supported the relevance of NRF2-associated states to treatment-response biology, while also indicating limited utility for static pan-cancer prediction. Exploratory whole-slide image analyses using pathology foundation-model embeddings identified morphology associations with myeloid, hypoxic, and CAF/TGF-beta barrier programs. VISTA provides an evidence-layered approach to variant-informed tissue-state modeling. By integrating genomic, transcriptomic, imaging, spatial, cellular, dependency, and pharmacogenomic evidence, it can help prioritize genotype-linked cancer states and validation-ready hypotheses. VISTA is not intended to function as a stand-alone clinical predictor; its claims are bounded by the evidence available in each data layer and by the biological and clinical context of the analyzed cohorts.

title: P4HA1⁺ collagen-modifying fibroblasts are associated with pro-tumor niches and therapeutic vulnerabilities in colorectal cancer.
abstract: Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) are a major stromal component of the tumor microenvironment (TME) and actively participate in tumor progression. Although CAF heterogeneity in colorectal cancer (CRC) is increasingly recognized, how individual CAF subpopulations simultaneously coordinate extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling, angiogenesis, and immune suppression within spatially organized niches remains poorly understood. CAF heterogeneity was systematically analyzed by integrating single-cell RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, and bulk transcriptomic data. By combining cell clustering, pseudotime analysis, transcriptional regulatory network inference, spatial deconvolution, and ligand-receptor interaction analysis, we revealed the spatial distribution and cellular communication characteristics of CAF subpopulations. At the same time, machine learning-based prognostic models and transcriptional perturbation analysis were used to evaluate the clinical significance and potential therapeutic value of CAF-related transcriptional programs. We identified a prolyl 4-hydroxylase subunit alpha 1 (P4HA1)-positive collagen-modifying CAF subpopulation (P4HA1⁺ CAFs) that was enriched in tumor tissue and exhibited collagen remodeling characteristics. This subpopulation preferentially localized at the tumor-stroma interface, co-localizing with pro-angiogenic endothelial cells, immunosuppressive macrophages, and malignant epithelial cells to form a spatially organized niche with concurrent ECM remodeling, angiogenesis, and immune suppression. P4HA1⁺ CAFs were predicted to engage distinct ligand-receptor axes, including WNT5A-MCAM with endothelial cells, MDK-LRP1 with macrophages, and MDK-NCL with malignant epithelial cells. The MDK-NCL axis was associated with increased RANBP1 expression and enhanced tumor cell proliferation and invasion. Machine learning analysis further identified P4HA1, TIMP1, ARL4C, and SFRP4 as stable core genes associated with poor prognosis. Drug perturbation analysis showed that 2-methoxyestradiol and its combination with the histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor JNJ-26,481,585 may partially reverse the malignant transcriptional program of P4HA1⁺ CAFs. This study characterizes a P4HA1⁺ collagen-modifying CAF subpopulation that resides within a spatially organized multicellular niche and engages distinct signaling axes to simultaneously promote angiogenesis, immune suppression, and tumor cell proliferation in CRC, highlighting its prognostic and potential therapeutic value.

title: Epigenetic regulation of INPP5D and its downstream molecular network in autoimmune pancreatitis.
abstract: Autoimmune pancreatitis (AIP) is a representative manifestation of IgG4-related disease characterized by lymphoplasmacytic inflammation and storiform fibrosis. Although epigenetic dysregulation has been implicated in autoimmune diseases, its contribution to the pathogenesis of AIP remains unclear. Genome-wide DNA methylation profiling was performed using the Infinium MethylationEPIC array in tissues affected by AIP and obstructive pancreatitis (OP). Differentially methylated regions (DMRs) were identified and subjected to pathway enrichment analysis. Among the significantly enriched gene sets, GNF2_INPP5D showed the strongest enrichment and was selected for further investigation. INPP5D promoter methylation was analyzed, and its protein expression was evaluated by immunohistochemistry. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) was performed to identify the cells expressing INPP5D. Pathway enrichment analysis showed significant enrichment of the INPP5D-associated immune-regulatory network in AIP. Promoter-associated CpG probes within the INPP5D locus showed predominant hypomethylation in AIP compared with the findings in OP (adjusted p < 0.05). In contrast, immunohistochemistry demonstrated reduced INPP5D expression in spindle-shaped stromal macrophage/histiocyte-lineage cells in AIP tissues. scRNA-seq analysis identified INPP5D expression predominantly in C1QC-positive macrophages and lymphocytes. AIP is characterized by epigenetic remodeling of the INPP5D-associated immune-regulatory network accompanied by reduced INPP5D expression in stromal macrophage-lineage cells. These findings provide evidence for an association between altered INPP5D-related epigenetic regulation and the characteristic fibro-inflammatory microenvironment of AIP. INPP5D may represent a candidate biomarker and a potential therapeutic target in IgG4-related disease.

title: Applications of single-cell RNA sequencing in fungal infections.
abstract: Fungal infection elicits markedly different cellular responses depending on the pathogen, tissue involved, host immune status, and stage of disease. Bulk measurements capture broad changes but can obscure the cell populations associated with fungal control, persistence, or tissue injury. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) offers a way to resolve this heterogeneity, although fungal infection studies remain uneven in both technical feasibility and disease coverage. We review evidence from cutaneous, mucosal, pulmonary, central nervous system, and systemic infections, with attention to tissue context, experimental design, and the strength of supporting validation. Across these studies, myeloid, lymphoid, epithelial, and stromal compartments show substantial remodeling, yet similarly named cell states do not necessarily have equivalent functions in different tissues or infections. Direct fungal single-cell studies are fewer, but they reveal variation in developmental stage, morphogenesis, stress responses, and responses to antifungal exposure. Most evidence still centers on Candida, whereas studies of Aspergillus, Cryptococcus, Pneumocystis, Coccidioides, and chronic cutaneous mycoses remain restricted to particular models or sample types. Interpretation is complicated by dissociation-related bias, unequal cell recovery, sparse fungal RNA, cross-species mapping, and small human cohorts. Spatial and functional validation are therefore important for distinguishing transcriptional associations from mechanisms. At present, single-cell approaches are most useful for defining context-dependent states and generating mechanistic questions; broader clinical application will require standardized sampling, independent validation, and scalable assays.

title: Genetic susceptibility and clinical validation of ICAM-5 in immune-mediated non-infectious uveitis.
abstract: To investigate genetically supported molecular factors associated with uveitis and to evaluate the clinical, transcriptomic, and retinal relevance of intercellular adhesion molecule 5 (ICAM-5) across major immune-mediated non-infectious uveitis subtypes. Two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) was conducted using eQTLGen eQTL data and two independent pQTL resources (Icelandic SomaScan and FinnGen R10), with uveitis GWAS summary statistics as the outcome. ICAM5 was evaluated using complementary MR estimators, sensitivity analyses, reverse MR, and Bayesian colocalization. Plasma ICAM-5 concentrations were measured by ELISA in 90 patients with active non-infectious uveitis (30 each with Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada disease, Behçet's disease-associated uveitis, and HLA-B27-associated acute anterior uveitis) and 40 healthy controls using age- and sex-adjusted models. ICAM5 expression was further examined in the peripheral-blood transcriptomic dataset GSE194060, whereas retinal Icam5 expression and cellular distribution were evaluated using experimental autoimmune uveitis retinal single-cell RNA-sequencing data and GSE132229. Genetically predicted higher ICAM5 expression and ICAM-5 protein levels were associated with increased uveitis susceptibility in the eQTLGen dataset (OR = 2.46, 95% CI 1.48-4.11, P = 5.69 × 10-4; nSNP =8), the Icelandic SomaScan cis-pQTL analysis (OR = 1.27, 95% CI 1.11-1.46, P = 5.30 × 10-4; nSNP =89), and the FinnGen R10 cis-pQTL analysis (OR = 1.21, 95% CI 1.07-1.38, P = 3.13 × 10-³; nSNP =4). Sensitivity analyses showed no significant heterogeneity or horizontal pleiotropy, and reverse MR provided no evidence of an association from uveitis liability to ICAM-5 levels. Plasma ICAM-5 concentrations were higher in all three uveitis subgroups than in healthy controls and remained elevated after age and sex adjustment, with the greatest increase in Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada disease. In the GSE194060 peripheral-blood transcriptomic dataset, ICAM5 expression was higher in the uveitis group. Analysis of the retinal single-cell RNA-sequencing data showed that Icam5 was predominantly detected in neuronal populations. Multi-omics MR, clinical protein quantification, transcriptomic analysis, and retinal single-cell profiling provide convergent evidence linking ICAM-5 to immune-mediated non-infectious uveitis. These findings support ICAM-5 as a genetically supported candidate mediator and circulating biomarker.

title: Integrated multi-omics and machine learning identify core mechanobiology-associated immune genes in pulmonary arterial hypertension.
abstract: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) involves vascular remodeling and altered mechanical signaling. The immune-associated transcriptomic changes accompanying this environment remain incompletely characterized. We integrated bulk lung (GSE15197), PBMC (GSE33463), and single-cell RNA-seq (GSE169471) data using a curated set of 2, 537 mechanical-related genes. WGCNA, LASSO, random forest, and single-cell localization supported candidate prioritization. The four-gene panel was examined in a monocrotaline-induced PH rat model and PBMCs from 10 IPAH patients and 10 controls. PAH transcriptomes showed enrichment of stress-fiber, actomyosin, ECM, and immune-related programs. CD83, CD86, IL6, and TLR7 were prioritized, with compartment-dependent expression patterns. Single-cell data localized CD83/CD86 to myeloid/APC compartments and IL6 to endothelial/fibroblast populations; TLR7 was sparsely detected. In MCT-treated rat lungs, CD86 and TLR7 proteins increased, whereas CD83 and IL-6 decreased. Clinical PBMCs showed corresponding expression directions, and each gene had an AUC >0.7. The exploratory four-gene disease-state score achieved an internal cross-validated AUC of 0.765. The four candidates provide a cellular and molecular context for investigating immune-stromal interactions in PAH, including responses to noninfectious vascular injury. The panel showed moderate internal discrimination. These findings support further clinical and functional investigation but do not establish direct mechanotransduction targets or a causal pathway linking mechanical stress to vascular inflammation.

title: Integrating Mendelian randomization with single-cell and spatial transcriptomics to investigate gut microbiota-associated genetic signals and molecular characteristics in prostate cancer.
abstract: Prostate cancer (PRAD) represents one of the most prevalent malignancies among men globally. Accumulating evidence implicates gut microbiota dysbiosis in the initiation and progression of prostate cancer; however, the causal relationship and underlying molecular mechanisms remain incompletely elucidated. This study integrated Mendelian randomization (MR), bioinformatics, single-cell RNA sequencing, and spatial transcriptomics to systematically investigate the genetic associations between gut microbiota and prostate cancer risk and characterize the expression patterns of microbiota-associated candidate genes within the tumor microenvironment. Two-sample MR analyses were performed using summary statistics from the OpenGWAS database to evaluate causal associations between gut microbiota and PRAD risk, with sensitivity analyses conducted to ensure robustness. Significant SNPs were functionally annotated and mapped to candidate genes using g:SNPense, and differentially expressed associated genes (DEAGs) were identified through integration with GEO datasets. Subsequent analyses encompassed immune infiltration profiling, machine learning model construction, and nomogram validation. Single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics were employed to delineate cell type-specific expression and spatial distribution patterns of signature genes. Candidate gene expression alterations in prostate cancer cells were experimentally validated by quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR). MR analyses identified significant positive causal associations between PRAD risk and Brevibacillaceae, Brevibacillales, CAG-110, and Pararhizobium, whereas Lawsonibacter sp000492175 exhibited a significant inverse association. A total of 21 differentially expressed genes were identified, with RASSF3, CROCC, UBE4B, SMOC2, and ACACA emerging as key signature genes. Immune infiltration analyses revealed a significant positive correlation between FRMD3 and regulatory T cells (Tregs), and a negative correlation between ACACA and neutrophil infiltration. The random forest classifier demonstrated optimal predictive performance, achieving an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.853 in the validation cohort. Single-cell and spatial transcriptomic analyses revealed cell-type-associated expression patterns of ACACA, SMOC2, and UBE4B across different cellular populations. These findings suggest potential associations between signature genes and specific cellular contexts, which require further experimental validation. qRT-PCR validated differential expression patterns of these candidate genes in prostate cancer cells. This study provides genetic causal inference evidence supporting a close association between gut microbiota and prostate cancer risk, and identifies multiple key signature genes implicated in immune microenvironment regulation and tumor progression. Integrated single-cell and spatial transcriptomic analyses suggest that these genes exhibit distinct expression patterns among different cellular populations and may provide clues for understanding their potential roles in PRAD progression. These findings provide genetic evidence supporting the association between gut microbiota and prostate cancer risk and highlight potential microbiota-associated molecular signatures. Further functional studies are required to clarify whether these genes directly contribute to microbiota-related prostate cancer progression.

title: Evaluating [18F]-AlF-FAPI-74 PET/CT for diagnosis of the unfavourable CMS4 colorectal cancer subtype (FoCus study): protocol for a prospective, observational, proof-of-concept clinical study.
abstract: Consensus molecular subtype 4 (CMS4) colorectal cancer (CRC) is characterised by stromal activation, therapy resistance and poor prognosis. Current CMS4 assessment relies on tissue sampling, which is limited by sampling bias due to inter-lesion and intra-lesion heterogeneity. Fibroblast activation protein (FAP) gene-expression is strongly associated with CMS4 status. [18F]-AlF-FAPI-74 positron emission tomography (PET)/ computed tomography (CT) enables non-invasive, whole-body assessment of FAP expression and may therefore provide an imaging-based biomarker for CMS4 status in CRC. FoCus is a prospective, observational proof-of-concept clinical study including 45 patients (≥18 years) with resectable metachronous or synchronous colorectal liver metastases. Eligible patients must have at least one liver metastasis of ≥15 mm scheduled for surgical resection. Patients will undergo [18F]-AlF-FAPI-74 PET/CT prior to clinically indicated therapeutic interventions, including surgical resection of primary tumours and/or metastases and, when applicable, prior to systemic therapy. The primary endpoint is CMS4 status, determined by RNA sequencing of resected tumour tissue using multi-region sampling to account for spatial heterogeneity. Diagnostic performance of FAPI-PET (index test) for CMS4 classification (reference standard) will be evaluated using receiver operating characteristic analysis at the tumour-level. Secondary endpoints include FAP expression assessed by immunohistochemistry and ELISA. The study has been approved by the institutional review board NedMec+, the Netherlands (protocol 23-298; Clinical Trials Information System EU CT number: 2023-509183-17-00). All participants will provide written informed consent. Results will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications and scientific conferences. NCT06191120.

title: UBL3 Modification Reduces Nuclear POLE Levels to Potentiate Antitumor Immunity in Aero-upper Digestive Squamous Cell Carcinomas.
abstract: While immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have revolutionized treatment of the patients with aero-upper digestive squamous cell carcinomas (SCCs), including esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) and lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC), only a subset of patients benefit from ICIs, therefore entailing exploration of the mechanisms to regulate treatment responsiveness. POLE, as a subunit of DNA polymerase ε, possesses 3'-5' proofreading activity, and its mutations have been associated with favourable response to ICIs in several solid tumors. However, post-translational modification (PTM) of POLE and its impact on the therapeutic efficacy of ICIs are unknown. Here, this study demonstrates that ubiquitin-like protein 3 (Ubl3), whose expression is markedly downregulated in SCCs, covalently binds to Pole, reduces nuclear Pole levels, triggers DNA damage, and activates cGAS-STING signaling pathway. Notably, Ubl3 modification of Pole significantly primes the local immune microenvironment to mitigate the growth of murine aero-upper digestive SCC cells and boost the efficacy of αPD-1 treatment in vivo. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis further revealed that UBL3 expression is positively correlated with better clinical outcomes in a cohort of ESCC patients receiving neoadjuvant chemotherapy combined with αPD-1. Together, our findings unravel UBL3 modification as a novel PTM mechanism governing subcellular location of POLE and its influence on immunotherapy responsiveness, thus making UBL3 modification as a promising immunomodulatory approach to enhance immunotherapy efficacy in patients with aero-upper digestive SCCs.

title: Metabolic reprogramming of NK cells in chronic brucellar arthritis: role of the HIF-1α/mTOR axis.
abstract: Brucellar arthritis is the most common complication of brucellosis, and its chronic progression is closely associated with immune cell dysfunction. Natural killer (NK) cells play a central role in anti-infective immunity; however, their functional status and regulatory mechanisms in brucellar arthritis remain poorly understood. Peripheral blood and synovial tissue samples were collected from healthy controls, as well as from patients with acute-phase and chronic-phase brucellar arthritis. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), flow cytometry, quantitative real-time PCR (qPCR), JC-1 mitochondrial membrane potential assay, Seahorse metabolic analysis, and Western blotting were employed to systematically evaluate NK cell phenotypes, functions, metabolic profiles, and HIF-1α/mTOR pathway activity. In vitro, heat-killed Brucella melitensis 16M (HKBA) was used to stimulate NK-92 cells and HIF-1α-knockout (KO) cell lines, with mTOR inhibitor intervention, to dissect the regulatory mechanism of the HIF-1α/mTOR axis in NK cell metabolic reprogramming. scRNA-seq revealed enrichment of NK cells in the synovium of brucellar arthritis patients, with aberrant expression of oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS)-related genes. Clinical sample analyses showed that, compared with healthy controls, the proportion of peripheral blood NK cells increased in both acute- and chronic-phase patients; however, NK cells from chronic-phase patients exhibited significantly reduced IFN-γ, Granzyme B, and CD107a degranulation levels. HIF-1α protein was consistently overexpressed in patient NK cells, whereas phosphorylated mTOR-pathway proteins (p-PI3K, p-AKT, p-mTOR) were markedly suppressed. In vitro, HKBA treatment inhibited mTOR pathway activity in NK-92 cells in a dose- and time-dependent manner and reduced mitochondrial membrane potential as shown by JC-1 staining. HIF-1α knockout significantly restored NK cell cytotoxic function, upregulated OXPHOS- and glycolysis-related gene expression, and improved mitochondrial membrane potential. Transcriptomic sequencing confirmed enrichment of mTOR signaling and energy metabolism gene sets after knockout. Importantly, mTOR pathway inhibition completely blocked the HIF-1α-knockout-mediated restoration of NK cell function and mitochondrial fitness, indicating that HIF-1α primarily drives NK cell metabolic and functional abnormalities through mTOR suppression. Brucella infection induces HIF-1α overexpression, which suppresses mTOR signaling and drives metabolic reprogramming of NK cells characterized by impaired OXPHOS and functional exhaustion, thereby promoting chronicity of brucellar arthritis. Targeting the HIF-1α/mTOR axis may offer a novel therapeutic strategy for brucellar arthritis.
